cover.headline: No turnaround yet, but priced for permanent decline: 11x earnings, a 5% yield and net cash
cover.lead: Wipro is India's fourth-largest IT services company ($10.5 bn of revenue, ~243,000 staff), controlled by the Premji family (72.6%). Its constant-currency revenue fell in each of the last three years (−4.4%, −2.3%, −1.6%), Q1FY27 grew only 0.9% with two acquisitions included, and the Q2 guide (−1.5% to +0.5% QoQ) implies organic decline; the IT Services margin slipped to 16.0%, below the 17-17.5% band management wants back. In June Wipro bought back 6% of its shares at ₹250; by 30-Sep-2026 the stock was ₹158.5, down ~40% in 2026 with the whole sector on fears that AI shrinks traditional IT work, and it left the Nifty 50 that day. The street values Wipro on **P/E (10-15x FY28E EPS)**. We forecast EPS of ₹13.3 in FY27E and ₹13.9 in FY28E, a little below the street. Applying **14x to Sep-28E EPS of ₹14.5** gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with BUY**, on valuation and yield, not on a turnaround. Cross-checks: EV/EBITDA ₹200, DCF ₹252. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Dollar revenue has fallen from $11.23 bn (FY23) to $10.48 bn (FY26). We forecast -0.5% in FY27E even with ~3 pp from DTS and Mindsprint, so the underlying business shrinks ~3%. Americas 2 (banks, insurers, energy) fell 7.3% YoY in Q1; growth comes only from Europe and APMEA, partly bought.

arguments.h: AI is eating the run business
arguments.p: Management says clients' traditional IT, BPO and support budgets are "getting compressed" and that cost-takeout deals carry forward productivity and lower margins. Headcount fell ~2,500 in Q1 excluding Mindsprint. Peers that grow are those with more engineering and AI work; Wipro discloses no AI revenue.

arguments.h: Margins: below the band, and staying there
arguments.p: IT Services EBIT margin 17.2% in FY26, 16.0% in Q1FY27 (wage hike, deal ramp-ups, AI-native unit). Management gave no date for a return to 17-17.5%. We model 16.3% / 16.6% / 16.8% (company basis) for FY27-29E, at the low end of the street.

At ₹158.5 the stock trades at 11.4x our FY28E EPS (median since 2021: 19.5x) with a ~5.0% FY27E dividend yield. A DCF at 11.9% equals the price only if rupee cash flows shrink ~2% a year forever. Even after cutting its post-2021 median by the peers' ~29% de-rating, our 14x gives {{dcf.tp|inr}}. The risk is a value trap if dollar revenue keeps shrinking (bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}).

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-October 2026): delivery against the −1.5% to +0.5% QoQ guide, the Q3 guide, and whether the margin climbs back from 16.0%.
Deal conversion: Q1 bookings were $3.4 bn (−32% YoY) with decisions slipping into Q2; ramp-up of the Americas BFSI and European EMR wins management pointed to.
AI pricing: how much productivity Wipro gives back on renewals, and whether it starts disclosing AI revenue as TCS, Infosys and HCLTech do.
US macro and policy: a Fed that hiked in September, 10-year yields near 5%, the extended $100,000 H-1B fee; Accenture's Aug-quarter results (due in early October).
Capital return: the January interim dividend (₹2 declared in July vs ₹5 a year earlier) and any new buyback under the 70% payout policy.

sections.title: A $10.5 bn IT services firm: run-the-business work for 1,233 clients, a third of it for banks

blocks.p: Wipro writes, runs and maintains software and IT systems for large companies, mostly in the US and Europe, from delivery centres in India (60% of service revenue is earned offshore). Its work spans application development and maintenance, cloud and infrastructure management, enterprise software (SAP, Oracle, Salesforce), engineering services for technology and manufacturing clients (boosted by the DTS acquisition from Harman in Dec-2025), business process services, cybersecurity and consulting through **Capco**, a banking-focused consultancy. Almost all revenue (99%+) is **IT Services**, reported in dollars; **IT Products** (reselling software) was only ₹694 cr in FY26. More than half the work is fixed-price (53.6% in Q1FY27), so Wipro keeps the productivity gains it delivers on time and absorbs the overruns.

blocks.callout: **Corporate actions and per-share data:** the 1:1 bonus in Dec-2024 doubled the share count; Screener restates all earlier EPS for it (FY24 ₹10.57 = ₹21.1 before the bonus), so the per-share history in this report is consistent. The June-2026 buyback cut shares from 1,050.4 cr to 990.4 cr. Our model puts FY26 on that post-buyback count: pro-forma EPS ₹13.33 against ₹12.58 reported (₹12.60 under IFRS), and the Mar-26 balance sheet less the ₹15,000 cr paid out and ~₹4,435 cr spent on acquisitions after March. Exceptional items are small (₹39 cr gain in FY26); restructuring charges in Q1 and Q3 FY26 and a labour-code charge in Q4FY26 sit inside operating costs.

sections.title: Indian IT: a $315 bn export industry growing in low single digits, with AI rewriting the price of its core work

blocks.p: Indian IT services companies sell engineers' time and outcomes to global corporations, mostly from India. The model worked for 30 years because Indian engineers cost a fraction of Western ones and clients kept outsourcing more. Nasscom put FY26 industry revenue at $315 bn (+6.1%) but headcount grew only 2.3%, and it flagged pricing compression. The large listed firms did worse: TCS −2.4% and Wipro −1.6% in constant currency in FY26, Infosys +3.1%, HCLTech +3.9%. FY27 guidance is 1.5-3.0% (Infosys, trimmed in July) and 1-4% (HCLTech). The 2025-26 slowdown has three causes at once: cautious client budgets (tariffs, the West Asia war, oil above $100, US rates near 5%), US visa costs, and generative/agentic AI, which lets clients do the same work with fewer people and asks the vendor to pass the savings on.

sections.title: Cyclical slowdown or lasting de-rating? Both, and Wipro is more exposed than most

blocks.p: This is the question that decides every Indian IT stock. By 30-Sep-2026 the Nifty IT index had fallen ~40% from its Dec-2024 peak (−27% in 2026 alone, −11% in September), and the large firms traded at 12-18x trailing earnings against 20-30x five-year medians. Two explanations compete. The **cyclical** one: clients froze discretionary budgets in a year of tariffs, war, oil shocks and rising US rates; when they thaw, growth and multiples recover, as after past downturns. The **structural** one: AI coding and agents do a growing share of the work Indian IT is paid for (maintenance, testing, support, BPO), clients demand the savings, and revenue per unit of work falls for years. The evidence below is dated to 30-Sep-2026.

blocks.h: What the market and the cycle tell us

bullets: Nifty IT peaked at ~46,000 in Dec-2024; touched 26,426 intraday on 30-Jun-2026, ~42% below the peak. (2026-06)

blocks.callout: **Our verdict:** both. The 2026 demand slump is partly cyclical (macro shocks, deal slippage, a client-specific issue at Wipro), and some of it will reverse. But AI pricing pressure is real, measurable (2-3% a year of deflation in brokers' and HCLTech's estimates, falling headcount at most large firms) and will not reverse with the cycle. That justifies a permanently lower multiple for traditional IT services than the 20-30x of 2021-24. Wipro is more exposed than Infosys or HCLTech and at least as exposed as TCS: a large run book, no disclosed AI offset, and no organic growth even before the AI scare. We therefore model ~2-3% annual dollar growth after FY27, margins below management's band, and a 14x multiple, ~29% below its post-2021 median, in line with the de-rating of its peers rather than a return to history.

sections.title: Markets and sectors: the Americas are shrinking; Europe and APMEA grow, partly through acquisitions

blocks.p: Wipro runs its client business through four Strategic Market Units (SMUs). **Americas 1** (35% of revenue: technology, communications, media, health and consumer clients in the US, Canada and Latin America) was flat in Q1FY27; technology & communications grew 10.8% but US health insurers and hospitals cut budgets (health −3.0% YoY). **Americas 2** (25%: banks, insurers, capital markets, energy and manufacturing) is the problem: −6.7% YoY in Q4FY26 and −7.3% in Q1FY27, on delayed ramp-ups of large banking deals and a client-specific loss that management says ended in Q1. **Europe** (27%) grew 6% YoY on banking deal ramps and DTS; **APMEA** (12%) grew 13.5%, helped by Mindsprint (Olam, Singapore) from May-2026. Europe and APMEA earned 12.7% and 14.6% segment margins in FY26 against 21.3% and 18.7% in the Americas, so the mix shift itself costs margin.

blocks.callout: **So what:** the dollar line is the honest measure of Wipro's business, and on our numbers it is roughly where it was in FY22 by FY29E. Rupee revenue still grows 4-7% a year because the rupee keeps falling. That flatters reported growth and margins, but it is not something Wipro controls, and a stronger rupee would cut our FY28E EPS by ~2.5% for every 1% move (our estimate: ~30 bp of margin plus the smaller rupee revenue base).

sections.title: Deals and people: bookings are decent, but fewer people are doing the work

blocks.p: Two sets of numbers tell us where revenue is heading. **Bookings** (total contract value signed) were strong in FY26: $16.4 bn, with $7.8 bn of large deals (+45% CC), a book-to-bill of ~1.6x. But they were front-loaded (H1FY26 $9.7 bn) and slowed to $3.3-3.5 bn a quarter since; Q1FY27's $3.37 bn was 32% below a year earlier, with some decisions slipping into Q2. Large cost-takeout and vendor-consolidation deals convert slowly and at low margins, and they include productivity give-backs. **People**: headcount was ~233,000 for two years, jumped to ~242,000 with DTS (Q3FY26) and to 243,044 with Mindsprint, but fell ~2,500 in Q1FY27 excluding Mindsprint. Utilisation is 83-84% (87.7% in Q1FY25), attrition is a manageable 13.9%. Revenue per average employee fell from ~$45,100 (FY25) to ~$44,100 (FY26).

blocks.callout: **What it means:** the fall in $100 mn+ clients from 22 to 16 in two years matters more than any single quarter: Wipro's biggest relationships are shrinking, and the large deals it wins are mostly cost-takeout contracts that replace old revenue at lower prices. Bookings need to stay above ~$4 bn a quarter for revenue to grow; they have not since Q2FY26.

sections.title: Competitive advantage: sticky clients and a strong balance sheet, but no edge that shows up in growth or margins

verdicts: 97-99% of revenue from existing clients; 714 clients above $1 mn; top client 4.4%, top 10 23.6%.
Revenue is recurring, but stickiness has not stopped three years of decline.
IT Services $10.5 bn vs TCS ~$30 bn, Infosys ~$20 bn; $100 mn+ clients fell from 22 (FY24) to 16.
Less able to fund AI platforms and win mega-deals than the top two.
Capco gives BFSI consulting access; BFSI is 34% of revenue but Wipro's BFSI grew 0% over eight quarters (Choice).
A real asset that has not yet translated into growth.
IT Services EBIT 16-17% vs ~21-25% at TCS/Infosys/HCLTech (Screener EBITDA margins FY26: Wipro 19.2%, TCS 27.1%, Infosys 23.7%, HCLTech 20.6%).
No cost advantage; margins are the industry's lower half.
Wipro Intelligence (WINGS, WEGA), AI-native unit (Apr-2026), Anthropic and OpenAI partnerships; no AI revenue disclosed.
Peers disclose AI revenue; Wipro asks investors to take it on trust.
Three CEOs since 2016 (Pallia since Apr-2024); strategy and go-to-market structure recast each time.
Execution risk is higher than at peers.
Net cash ~₹21,400 cr after the buyback (Screener basis, Jun-26); OCF 98-113% of net income.
Pays dividends and buybacks; no financial risk.

blocks.source: GAM research compilation (company filings, datasheets, calls and broker notes to Sep-2026; Screener.in for peers' margins)

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict: no moat beyond switching costs.** Clients rarely fire an incumbent IT vendor mid-contract, so 97-99% of Wipro's revenue repeats each year, and that is real. But every large Indian IT firm has the same advantage, and Wipro has none of the extras that make the leaders worth more: it is smaller than TCS and Infosys, earns 1-8 points lower EBITDA margins than HCLTech, Infosys and TCS, has lost six of its $100 mn+ clients in two years, and cannot yet show that its AI platforms win work. Its best assets are Capco and the balance sheet; neither has produced growth.

sections.title: A decade of 6% rupee growth, mostly from the rupee and acquisitions; dollar revenue has shrunk for three years

blocks.p: Wipro's revenue grew from ₹51,244 cr in FY16 to ₹92,624 cr in FY26, about 6.1% a year, and profit attributable to shareholders from ₹8,908 cr to ₹13,197 cr, about 4.0% a year. Most of the rupee growth came from two sources that are not organic demand: acquisitions (Capco and others lifted FY22 revenue 28%) and a weaker rupee (₹65-70 per dollar in FY17-20, ₹87.9 in FY26). In dollars, IT Services revenue peaked at $11.23 bn in FY23 and has fallen every year since, to $10.48 bn in FY26: −4.4%, −2.3% and −1.6% in constant currency. EPS (adjusted for the 2024 bonus) went from ₹9.85 in FY21 to ₹12.58 in FY26, 5% a year, helped by three buybacks.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** Wipro's accounts look stable (EBITDA margin 19-20%, profit up a little each year) only because three things have offset falling dollar revenue: a cheaper rupee, cost cuts (employee cost fell from 61% to 60% of revenue) and buybacks. None of these is growth. The business has not grown organically since FY23, and FY27 will be the fourth year in a row of falling organic dollar revenue on our numbers.

blocks.callout: **Why it matters:** Wipro guides one quarter at a time and usually lands inside the range, so the guide is a good read on demand. The Q2 midpoint (−0.5% QoQ CC) includes a full quarter of Mindsprint (two months were in Q1), which means the rest of the business is expected to shrink ~1% in the quarter (ICICI Securities estimates −1.3% organic). There is no sign yet of the turnaround that would justify a higher multiple; our base case assumes none.

sections.title: Capital allocation: generous returns, mixed acquisitions

blocks.p: Wipro is a cash machine: operating cash flow was ₹17,622 cr in FY24, ₹16,943 cr in FY25 and ₹14,932 cr in FY26 (113% of profit), against capex of only ₹1,000-1,600 cr a year. Most of that cash goes back to shareholders. Since FY20 Wipro has run four tender buybacks (₹10,500 cr in 2019, ₹9,500 cr in 2020-21, ₹12,000 cr in 2023 and ₹15,000 cr in June 2026) and raised dividends to ₹11 a share in FY26. Its policy since FY26 is to return at least 70% of net income over three years; it returned ~88% over FY24-26. The promoter group, which owns ~72.6%, receives most of it: it tendered ~42.8 cr shares (~₹10,700 cr) into the 2026 buyback.

blocks.callout: **The capital question:** returning cash is the right call for a business that does not need it, and buying back stock at ₹250 (~20x FY26 EPS, a ~22% premium to the ~₹204 price in the week it was announced) looks expensive with hindsight: the stock was ₹158.50 on 30 September. The weaker record is acquisitions: Capco has not turned Wipro's BFSI business into a grower, and FY27's growth depends on DTS and Mindsprint. We model no further buybacks or acquisitions, ~₹8 of dividends in FY27 and a 70% payout after that.

sections.title: Earnings quality: clean, cash-backed accounts; a fifth of profit is treasury income

bullets: **Cash backs profit.** Operating cash flow was 113% of attributable profit in FY26, 129% in FY25 and 160% in FY24; over FY15-26 it was ₹1,43,515 cr against ₹1,24,544 cr of profit. Capex is only 1.5-2% of revenue. FY26 conversion fell because trade receivables rose 15% on 4% revenue growth (AR FY26), which is worth watching.

**Other income is large.** ₹3,899 cr in FY26, 22% of pre-tax profit: interest ₹2,837 cr, fair-value gains on funds and start-up stakes ₹812 cr, FX gains ₹185 cr (AR FY26 note 23). It falls by ~₹1,300 cr a year after the June-2026 buyback and acquisitions, which is why our FY27E EPS barely grows despite a weaker rupee.

**Restructuring is a habit.** Reconciling items (outside the IT Services segment) cost ₹795 cr in FY26: restructuring charges in Q1 and Q3 and the new labour codes in Q4. Management treats them as one-offs; we treat severance as a recurring cost of shrinking the workforce.

**Goodwill is half of equity.** Goodwill was ₹40,436 cr at Jun-26 (from Capco, Rizing, DTS, Mindsprint and others) against attributable equity of ₹77,471 cr. No impairment so far; a write-down would not affect cash but would show that acquisitions destroyed value.

**Disclosure is good.** Wipro files with the SEC (NYSE: WIT), reports under IFRS and Ind AS, discloses dollar revenue, constant-currency growth, SMU and sector splits, bookings, utilisation and attrition every quarter. It does not disclose organic growth after the first quarter of an acquisition, or AI revenue.
**Minorities and put options.** Minorities are tiny (₹68 cr of FY26 profit); written put options to buy out partners in some acquisitions carry a ₹59 cr finance cost.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: GREEN.** Unqualified audit (Deloitte Haskins & Sells LLP), SEC-level disclosure, strong cash conversion and a simple, cash-rich balance sheet. Watch receivables, recurring "one-off" restructuring and the goodwill from acquisitions that have not produced growth.

sections.title: Net cash fell by half after the buyback but is still ~₹21,400 cr

blocks.p: At Mar-2026 Wipro held ₹57,342 cr of cash and investments (mostly Indian corporate bonds, mutual funds and deposits, plus ~₹2,160 cr of start-up stakes) against ₹20,291 cr of borrowings and leases, so net cash was ₹37,051 cr on Screener's basis. In June it paid ₹15,000 cr for the buyback and ~$474 mn for Mindsprint and two smaller deals; net cash was ₹21,420 cr at Jun-2026 (company balance sheet, same basis). Borrowings are short-term loans that fund working capital and hedging (the $750 mn bond due Jun-2026 was refinanced). Receivable days rose from 47 (FY24) to 54 (FY26), which is why cash conversion fell from 159% of profit in FY24 to 113%.

sections.title: Ownership: the Premji family controls 72.6%; domestic funds sold in 2026

blocks.p: The Premji family and its philanthropic entities own 72.59% (Jun-2026), mainly through three partnership firms (Zash, Prazim and Hasham Traders, ~60% between them), the Azim Premji Trust (6.5%) and Azim Premji personally (4.1%). Much of the dividend and buyback cash flows to the Azim Premji Foundation's work. Foreign investors own 8.85%, Indian institutions only 5.22% (7.9% in Mar-2026) and the public 13.21%. The free float is small (~27%), which limits index weights; Wipro left the Nifty 50 on 30-Sep-2026. Shareholder numbers jumped 17% to 30.4 lakh in the June quarter as retail investors bought around the buyback.

sections.title: The street: mostly Reduce or Sell, targets ₹150-210, all on P/E

blocks.p: At least 14 houses cut their targets after the Q1FY27 results on 16-Jul-2026 (Reuters: median target ₹187, from ₹210). Of the 14 views we collected, only Nomura, Nuvama and Deven Choksey rate it a Buy; Motilal Oswal and Axis are Neutral/Hold; PL, Emkay, Choice, ICICI Securities, Elara, Kotak, Jefferies and JPMorgan are Reduce, Sell or Underperform. Targets run from ₹150 to ₹210 (median ₹168, average ₹173), set when the stock was ~₹175-178; by 30-Sep-2026 it was ₹158.5. Every house that discloses a method uses **P/E, mostly on FY28E EPS, at 10-15x (clustered at 11-13x)**. No broker changed its view on fundamentals in Aug-Sep 2026 that we could find; JPMorgan reiterated Underweight (₹155) on 10-Sep. Bears cite the weakest growth among large peers, AI deflation, margins below the band and falling bookings; bulls cite the ~5% dividend yield, cheap valuation and margin normalisation.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a value stock, not a turnaround; BUY at 11.4x FY28E

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** a $10.5 bn IT services firm whose dollar revenue has shrunk for three years and will shrink again organically in FY27 on our numbers, with margins below management's own band and no disclosed AI offset. In exchange you get ~5.0% FY27E dividend yield, net cash of ~₹25 a share by Mar-27 (~16% of the price), ~17% ROE, clean accounts and an owner that returns 70-90% of profit.

**What you are paying:** 11.9x our FY27E and 11.4x FY28E EPS, near the bottom of its forward-P/E range since 2016 (lows of ~10x in 2016-20 and 8.4x in the Covid crash). The price implies rupee cash flows falling ~2% a year forever. On the street's method and the house's derivation the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): **BUY**, on valuation and yield, not on a turnaround. Most brokers are Reduce or Sell at 10-13x; our multiple is higher because we measure Wipro against its own history and the sector's de-rating, not against its recent momentum.

bullets: **Rating: BUY, target {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}).** Our ratings follow the upside to our 12−month target: BUY at +15% or more, HOLD between −5% and +15%, SELL below −5%.

**We would stay buyers below ~₹180** and turn sellers above ~₹215 on today's numbers. We would cut our forecasts, and move towards the bear case, if Q2-Q3FY27 show organic decline worse than ~1% a quarter or margins below 16%.

**Position size:** this is a cheap, cash-rich, shrinking business. It suits investors who want yield and mean reversion; it is not a growth or AI play. The bear case (₹{{scen.bear.tp|num}}) is a real possibility.
**Biggest swing factor:** the margin. Each 1pp of EBITDA margin is ~6% of our FY28E EPS and ~₹10 a share at our multiple.
